name: Hawaii

program.agency: Hawaii Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation, Crime Victim Compensation Commission
program.statute_citation: Haw. Rev. Stat. ch. 351; Haw. Admin. R. ch. 23-605

sources.title: Haw. Admin. R. Title 23, Chapter 605 (Crime Victims Compensation)
HRS 351-62 Limitations upon award of compensation
Department of the Attorney General: Hawaii Sexual Assault Response and Training (HSART) Program

rules.summary: The Attorney General's sexual assault response program page says a primary police role is to make sure victims are offered and given free forensic exams, whether or not they report to police. This is a program role statement, not a statute, and it does not say who pays or whether insurance can be billed.
rules.quote: The primary roles of the police are to ensure that victims are offered and provided free forensic examinations regardless if a police report is made
rules.pinpoint: Dept. of the Attorney General, HSART Program page, "Who We Are and What We Do"

rules.summary: The maximum award is $10,000; if compensable medical expenses exceed $10,000, the award can go up to $20,000 or the actual medical expenses, whichever is lower.
rules.quote: No compensation shall be awarded under this chapter in an amount in excess of $10,000; provided that, if a case involves compensable medical expenses in excess of $10,000, no compensation shall be awarded in excess of $20,000 or the actual amount of compensable medical expenses, whichever is lower.

rules.summary: The application must be filed within eighteen months after the date of injury; the commission may accept a later application for good cause.
rules.quote: No order for the payment of compensation shall be made under this chapter unless the application has been made within eighteen months after the date of injury, death, or property damage; provided that upon a showing of good cause, the commission may consider applications filed beyond this time period.

params.extension: good cause, which the commission's rules limit to a mental, physical or legal impairment; ignorance of the law, incarceration or negligence do not count

rules.summary: Under the commission's rules, good cause for filing after 18 months or reporting to police late means the applicant could not do it because of a mental, physical or legal impairment; not knowing the law, incarceration, or negligent failure to learn the facts is not good cause.
rules.quote: "Good cause" means a determination that the applicant was unable to file an application within 18 months after the date of the incident or report the incident to the police without undue delay due to a mental, physical or legal impairment. Good cause may not be established by ignorance of the law, incarceration, or negligent failure to ascertain the facts giving rise to a claim

rules.summary: No prosecution or conviction is needed, but an arrest must have been made or the crime must have been reported to police without undue delay.
rules.quote: An order may be made under this section whether or not any person is prosecuted for or convicted of a crime arising out of an act or omission described in subsection (a) if an arrest has been made or the act or omission has been reported to the police without undue delay.

rules.summary: The commission's rules define undue delay in reporting to police as 72 hours, and the commission may accept a later police report for good cause.
rules.quote: "Undue delay" means 72 hours, provided that upon a showing of good cause, the commission may consider a police

rules.summary: The commission deducts money received or to be received from other sources, such as the offender or public or private funds, that is tied to the injury.
rules.quote: In determining the amount of compensation to be awarded under this chapter, the commission shall deduct amounts or benefits received or to be received from any source, whether from the offender or from any person on behalf of the offender, or from public or private funds

rules.summary: The program calls itself the payor of last resort and pays after all other sources are used up.
rules.quote: is a “payor of last resort” and may pay compensation after all other sources have been exhausted.

rules.summary: The commission considers whether the victim shares responsibility for the crime and reduces the award in proportion.
rules.quote: the commission shall consider the behavior of the victim, and whether, because of provocation or otherwise, the victim bears any share of responsibility for the crime that caused the victim's injury or death and the commission shall reduce the amount of compensation in proportion to the amount of responsibility for the crime which caused the victim's injury or death

rules.summary: In sexual assault cases, an award may not be reduced or denied because of how the victim was dressed, where the victim was, the time of the assault, alcohol or drug use, or a previous sexual relationship with the offender.
rules.quote: Factors that shall not be considered in reducing or denying an award include, but are not limited to: (1) Cases involving sexual assault: (A) The manner in which the victim was dressed at the time of the assault; (B) Where the victim was prior to the sexual assault; (C) The time of the sexual assault; (D) Whether the victim was or may have been under the influence of alcohol or drugs; (E) Whether the victim had a previous sexual relationship with the offender;

rules.summary: Sexual assault in the first through fourth degree are covered crimes.
rules.quote: Sexual assault in the first degree (section 707-730); (13) Sexual assault in the second degree (section 707-731); (14) Sexual assault in the third degree (section 707-732); (15) Sexual assault in the fourth degree (section 707-733);

rules.summary: Sex trafficking is a covered crime.
rules.quote: Sex trafficking (section 712-1202)

params.rule: Any private citizen hurt by a crime within Hawaii's criminal jurisdiction; Hawaii residents hurt in another state by a listed crime; Hawaii residents hurt by terrorism outside the United States.

rules.summary: Anyone hurt by a covered crime within Hawaii's criminal jurisdiction can apply, and Hawaii residents hurt by a covered crime in another state can also apply.
rules.quote: In the event any private citizen is injured or killed by any act or omission of any other person coming within the criminal jurisdiction of the State after June 6, 1967, or any state resident is injured or killed by any act or omission of any other person after July 1, 1989, in another state, which act or omission is within the description of the crimes enumerated in section 351-32

rules.summary: Medical expenses directly related to the crime are covered, including hospitalization.
rules.quote: Medical expenses are those expenses directly related to the incident that may include: (1) Hospitalization;

rules.summary: Prescription drugs are a covered medical expense.
rules.quote: (5) Prescription drugs;

rules.summary: Prescription eyeglasses, contact lenses, dentures and prosthetics are a covered medical expense if they were damaged in the crime.
rules.quote: (6) Prescription eyeglasses, contact lens, dentures, and prosthetics if damaged in the crime;

rules.summary: Mental health expenses are listed as a covered crime-related expense.
rules.quote: Medical and mental health expenses

rules.summary: Dental expenses are listed as covered.
rules.quote: Dental expenses

rules.summary: The commission may pay for the victim's loss of earning power from total or partial incapacity.
rules.quote: Loss to the victim of earning power as a result of total or partial incapacity;

rules.summary: The commission may pay for the victim's pain and suffering; the program calls this a one-time Acknowledgement Award.
rules.quote: Pain and suffering to the victim;

rules.summary: The reasonable replacement or rental cost of items taken as evidence can be covered as an other monetary loss, with verification. This rule is limited to items taken as evidence; it is not a general property replacement benefit.
rules.quote: Verification is required to establish other monetary losses and may include, but not limited to: (1) Reasonable cleaning of the crime scene; (2) Reasonable replacement or rental cost for items taken as evidence;

rules.summary: Reasonable cleaning of the crime scene can be covered as an other monetary loss, with verification.
rules.quote: (1) Reasonable cleaning of the crime scene;

rules.summary: Replacement dependent care can be covered when the victim's attending medical or other service provider supports the need.
rules.quote: (4) Replacement for dependent care or independent living support when evidenced by the attending medical or

params.item: property damage, except in Good Samaritan claims

rules.summary: The program lists property damage as covered only for Good Samaritans, so property damage to a crime victim (for example a phone or other belongings) is not listed as covered, apart from items taken as evidence.
rules.quote: Property damage (“Good Samaritans” only)

params.item: any injury suffered while confined in a jail, prison or other correctional facility

rules.summary: No compensation is paid for an injury suffered while confined in a jail, prison or other correctional facility.
rules.quote: No compensation of any kind shall be awarded to a victim or intervenor who suffered injury or death while confined in any federal, state, or county jail, prison, or other correctional facility.

params.item: therapy sessions the victim or applicant does not show up for

rules.summary: The commission's rules say charges for therapy sessions the victim or applicant misses are not normally considered customary therapy expenses.
rules.quote: Sessions in which the victim or applicant fails to show up;

not_found: reporting alternatives for sexual assault (forensic exam, advocate, protective order)
coverage.notes: No Hawaii statute was found that says who pays for a sexual assault forensic exam or whether insurance may be billed; the only official statement found is the Attorney General HSART program page saying police are to ensure free exams regardless of reporting. No per-expense caps, minimum loss, or emergency award were found in HRS ch. 351 or HAR ch. 23-605; HAR 23-605-15 says administrative award guidelines may be set by the commission, but none were found published. No police-report alternative for sexual assault was found: HRS 351-31(d) requires an arrest or a police report without undue delay (72 hours under HAR 23-605-2, with a good cause exception). The 18 month filing deadline is stored as params.months because the schema has only years or days.

researcher_notes: Statute text is from capitol.hawaii.gov (HRS current). HAR ch. 23-605 is an OCR'd 2001 PDF hosted by the Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation; quotes were taken only from clean stretches, and garbled passages (the four-day lost earnings limit without a medical certificate in 23-605-12(c), and the therapy exclusions in 23-605-10(c)) were left out. HAR 23-605-6(a) limits out-of-state claims by Hawaii residents to states without an eligible compensation program, which HRS 351-31(a) does not say; the statute was used. The CVCC brochure PDF (Compensation_Brochure_2026c.pdf) extracts as font-encoded garbage, so it was not saved or quoted; its deadline sentence could not be read. The $10,000 cap in HRS 351-62(b) is the current statute text as retrieved; the medical-expense exception raises it to at most $20,000. The Acknowledgement Award on the CVCC page cites HRS 351-33(4) (pain and suffering). The Sex Abuse Treatment Center (a Hawaii Pacific Health program, not a state agency) states its medical forensic exam is free; it was not used as a rule source. Reviewer (Oct 3): HI-EXAM-1 rests only on the AG HSART page's description of the police role; a search and a check of Act 113 (2018) and HRS 844D-24 found no Hawaii statute saying who pays for the forensic exam or barring bills to the victim or insurer. The 18 month deadline is stored as params.months (not a schema key); the engine must read it. The 72 hour police-report window is stored without within_days because the source states hours, not days. HAR 23-605-12(c) appears to limit lost earnings to four days without a medical certificate, but the OCR is garbled so it is not quoted.
